title: Concurrency Patterns: select, sync, and Races

questions.prompt: When several cases of a `select` are ready at once, what happens?

options.text: It chooses one of the ready cases at random
It always runs the first case listed

questions.explanation: `select` picks one ready case at random, which helps prevent any single channel from starving the others.

questions.prompt: How do you make a `select` non-blocking?
questions.explanation: A `default` case runs immediately when no other case is ready, making the select non-blocking.

questions.prompt: Which three conditions together define a data race? Select all that apply.

options.text: Two goroutines access the same memory concurrently
At least one access is a write
There is no synchronization ordering the accesses

questions.explanation: A data race is concurrent access to the same memory, at least one being a write, with no synchronization — undefined behavior. All-reads is safe.

questions.prompt: You detect data races by running your program or tests with the ____ flag.
questions.explanation: The `-race` flag instruments memory accesses and reports races on executed paths; absence of a report is not proof there is no race.

questions.prompt: What problem does a worker pool solve?

options.text: It bounds parallelism by using a fixed set of goroutines to drain a jobs channel
It removes the need for channels
It makes all goroutines run on one core

questions.explanation: A worker pool caps how many goroutines run at once, so a huge number of jobs doesn't spawn unbounded goroutines.

questions.prompt: Match each sync tool to what it does.

pairs.right: A channel that fires after a duration (for timeouts)

questions.explanation: Mutex serializes access, RWMutex favors reads, Once runs setup once, and time.After powers select timeouts.
